title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Oxfordshire–Uxbridge Decision Brief
text: Purpose and companion files. This brief is prepared for the consultancy economics team and Dr John Nellthorp (ITS, University of Leeds). It sets out a concise, first-principles active travel uptake method aligned with Active Mode Benefits: Theoretical Framework (Nellthorp et al. 2026), illustrates it on the 112.5 km Oxfordshire-to-Uxbridge section, and highlights eight modelling decisions to agree before scaling to the full 805.6 km North–South Greenway. Prototype audits, full PCT/Bass equations, supplementary diagnostics, and the 4-table data contract sit in the Technical Appendix.

title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Oxfordshire–Uxbridge Decision Brief
text:
1 Executive Summary & Decisions to Agree

Corridor exposure matters: Attenuating Go Dutch by alignment and access distance (\(\omega_{ij}\)) with \(\kappa = 0.50\) reduces 3 km catchment uptake from +16,336 (unattenuated ceiling) to +4,096 new commute cyclists (11.6% mode share), of whom +2,454 (60%) sit on tightly aligned core OD pairs.
E-bikes unlock rural inter-town links: Conventional cycling peaks at 2–6 km, whereas e-bikes unlock 6–15 km market-town corridors (King's Sutton–Banbury, Wendover–Aylesbury, Chalfont St Peter–Uxbridge).
Leisure & ramp-up shift the BCR materially: Commuting is only 29.9% of cycling trips nationally; omitting leisure understates rural greenway demand 3–5×, while a realistic 5-year behavioural ramp-up reduces 40-year commute PVB by 12.0% (from £103.3m to £91.0m on the core commute subset).
Clear separation for appraisal: Route diversion, car/PT mode shift, and newly generated Exercise & Pleasure trips (\(VTT = 0\)) are kept strictly separate to comply with Nellthorp et al. (2026) double-counting rules.





Table 1: Eight methodological choices to confirm before scaling to the 805.6 km North–South Greenway.












#
Decision Area
Options to Consider
Recommended Default & Rationale




1
Commute baseline & WFH
(a) 2011 Census unadjusted; (b) 2021 Census; (c) 2011 spatial OD scaled to 2026 jobs and post-COVID office days
Option (c): avoids 2021 lockdown distortion; reflects hybrid work via annual days (190-200 vs 220).


2
Uptake model at full scale
(a) Attenuated PCT OD framework; (b) Full netassign GC discrete choice; (c) Hybrid netassign delta-GC and prop_on_scheme driving unified logit
Option (c) for final business case (full Nellthorp et al. 2026 alignment); Option (a) as transparent benchmark.


3
Car-diversion share (MECs)
(a) AMAT national default (24% car + 6% taxi); (b) OD-specific proportional diversion; (c) Nested logit separating Walk/Cycle vs Car/PT
Report (a) as TAG Core and (b)/(c) as Sensitivity: rural links (59-62% car share) exceed urban defaults.


4
Leisure & tourism demand
(a) Empirical NTS/ALS multipliers; (b) Spatial gravity model (residents + stations + campsites) calibrated to trail counters; (c) ORVal integration
Option (b) splitting Other Non-Work Utility vs Exercise & Pleasure (VTT = 0, lower car diversion), cross-checked with (a).


5
Behavioural ramp-up lag
(a) AMAT instant 100% Year 1; (b) Linear 3-5 yr build-up; (c) Bass S-curve (Central 5-yr maturity) convolved with 5-yr health lag
Option (c): empirically grounded (Goodman et al. 2014) with 3-yr and 8-yr sensitivities to guard against optimism bias.


6
E-bike segmentation
(a) Pool all cycling as unpowered; (b) Explicit unpowered vs e-bike split (slope/distance elasticity, ~4.5-5.0 METs, ~18-20 km/h)
Option (b): recommended by Nellthorp et al. (2026, s4.2.3) and decisive on 6-15 km rural inter-town links.


7
Appraisal horizon & TATE3030
(a) AMAT 20-year; (b) ATE 40-year infrastructure horizon; (c) TAG A1.1 60-year; plus TATE3030 morbidity timing
Option (b) (40 years) as core with 20-year AMAT sensitivity; structure outputs with delta_met_wk for TATE3030.


8
Spatial aggregation
(a) Whole-corridor unified appraisal; (b) Modular Route Cases / Sections with cross-boundary trips allocated by prop_on_scheme
Option (b) summing cleanly to (a): supports phased local funding without double-counting cross-section trips.

title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Oxfordshire–Uxbridge Decision Brief
text:
2 First-Principles Uptake Method
Following Nellthorp et al. (2026) (§3.1.1), demand modelling and welfare valuation must be specified jointly using the same Generalised Cost (\(GC_r = -U_r / \beta\); Wardman and Toner (2020)) attributes on route \(r\) connecting \((i, j)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
GC_{ij,r} &= \sum_{n \in r} \Bigl( m\,v_t\,t_n + v_s\,s_n + v_e\,e_n + v_c\,c_n \Bigr) + \frac{U_{\text{pre}} + U_{\text{post}}}{\beta} \\
          &\approx \int_{0}^{T_r} \Bigl[ \beta + q(t) + e(t) \Bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t + \frac{U_{\text{pre}} + U_{\text{post}}}{\beta}
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
where \(t_n\) is travel time (access multiplier \(m = 2.0\)), \(s_n\) is perceived safety threat (the dominant cycling deterrent; Department for Transport (2024)), \(e_n\) is net physical exertion (MET-hours, lower for e-bikes), \(c_n\) is ambience and comfort (upgrading to an off-road segregated track is valued at 16.28 p/min in 2023 prices; Department for Transport (2025)), and \(q(t)\) captures continuous traffic/surface conditions (Kouwenhoven et al. 2023).
That cost reduction \(\Delta GC_{ij} < 0\) drives three margins that appraisal must keep separate:

Route choice (diversion): Existing cyclists switch from parallel A/B roads onto the greenway (\(\text{new trips} = 0\); Journey Ambience & external safety benefits only).
Mode choice (mode shift): Existing travellers switch from car, PT, or walking onto cycling (Rule-of-a-Half \(\Delta CS\), full TATE3030/AMAT health & absenteeism benefits, plus TAG Unit A5.4 car-diversion MECs).
Trip generation (induced demand): New utility or Exercise & Pleasure trips (Rule-of-a-Half \(\Delta CS\) with \(VTT = 0\) for Exercise & Pleasure, full health benefits, zero car decongestion MECs).

To avoid crediting 100% of an area-wide Go Dutch network scenario (Lovelace et al. 2017) to a single linear greenway, we attenuate each 2011 Census OD pair by a dimensionless corridor exposure weight \(\omega_{ij} \in [0, 1]\):
\[
\omega_{ij} = \phi_{ij} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{a_i + a_j}{L_a}\right)
\tag{2}\]
where \(\phi_{ij} \in [0, 1]\) is the desire-line share within a 1.5 km corridor buffer, \(a_i, a_j\) are endpoint centroid distances (m) to the spine, and \(L_a = 3{,}000\text{ m}\). Steady-state commute cyclists \(C^{1}_{ij}\) are then bounded between observed baseline \(C^{0}_{ij}\) and the PCT upper-envelope reference \(C^{\text{ref}}_{ij}\) (Go Dutch Central \(\kappa = 0.50\); E-bikes High \(\kappa = 0.60\)):
\[
C^{1}_{ij} = \min\!\Bigl(N_{ij},\; C^{0}_{ij} + \kappa\,\omega_{ij}\,\max\bigl(0,\; C^{\text{ref}}_{ij} - C^{0}_{ij}\bigr)\Bigr)
\tag{3}\]
Full PCT logistic equations and an audit of the existing railactive prototype scripts are given in Appendix §1–2.

title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Oxfordshire–Uxbridge Decision Brief
text:
3 Oxfordshire–Uxbridge Case Study (112.5 km)
We test the framework on the 112.5 km Oxfordshire-to-Uxbridge spine (v0.5.2, Sections 13 to 11, 234 links from Banbury via Brackley, Calvert, Aylesbury, Wendover, and Amersham to Uxbridge). Over 64% (72 km) consists of off-road or segregated assets (detailed breakdown in Appendix Table 2).








Figure 1: Oxfordshire–Uxbridge corridor case study: (A) Preferred alignment by infrastructure class and 3 km buffer; (B) 2011 Census LSOA commute uptake desire lines (Corridor Central >= 2.5 new cyclists; King’s Sutton to Banbury highlighted).





Across all inter-LSOA 2011 Census commute pairs (\(\le 20\text{ km}\)) within 3 km of the spine (3,657 OD pairs, 53,440 commuters; 59.1% car driver, 22.2% walking, 3.92% cycling), the core corridor-aligned subset (endpoints \(\le 1.5\text{ km}\), \(\phi_{ij} \ge 0.70\), distance \(1.5\text{–}20\text{ km}\)) isolates 1,463 pairs and 23,217 commuters (4.29% baseline cycling).

Three appraisal lessons emerge directly from Table 2 and Figure 2:

Exposure attenuation prevents over-claiming: Unattenuated Go Dutch (+16,336) overstates single-corridor impact; attenuating by \(\omega_{ij}\) yields +4,096 Central new cyclists (11.6% share), with 60% (+2,454) on tightly aligned core links (14.9% share).
Nodal clustering vs rural gaps: Commute demand clusters around Aylesbury, Banbury, Uxbridge/Denham, and Amersham; rural mid-corridor sections (Calvert–Finmere) depend heavily on leisure/tourism and e-bikes.
E-bikes shift the distance curve: Unpowered cycling peaks at 2–6 km, whereas e-bikes unlock the 6–15 km inter-settlement band.

title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Oxfordshire–Uxbridge Decision Brief
section: 4 Worked Example, Leisure Extension & Temporal Lag
text:
4 Worked Example, Leisure Extension & Temporal Lag

4.1 King’s Sutton to Banbury (E01027288 -> E01028435)

Observed 2011 baseline: \(N_{ij} = 55\) commuters (0 cyclists, 1 walker, 34 car drivers [61.8%%], 8 car passengers, 7 bus, 5 rail); \(d_{ij} = 7.84\text{ km}\), slope \(g_{ij} = 1.50\%\). Centroids sit 246 m and 400 m from the spine with \(\phi_{ij} = 1.00\), giving \(\omega_{ij} = 0.8064\).
PCT propensities & corridor uptake: Evaluating Equation 3 between observed baseline (0), Go Dutch (\(p^{\text{Dutch}} = 21.29\%\), 11.71 cyclists), and E-bikes (\(p^{\text{ebike}} = 31.82\%\), 17.50 cyclists) yields 4.72 steady-state commute cyclists (8.6% share) under Corridor Central (8.97 one-way trips/day at AMAT’s 1.9 return factor, 15,471 cycle-km/yr over 220 days) and 8.47 cyclists (16.09 trips/day) under Corridor High (E-bikes).
Car diversion sensitivity: Proportional non-cycle diversion implies 61.8% (2.92 cyclists) divert from car driver — more than double AMAT’s 24% national urban default (+6% taxi; Department for Transport (2025)).

Further diagnostic plots for this pair and three Buckinghamshire/Uxbridge comparisons appear in Appendix §3.


4.2 Extending to Leisure & Exercise/Pleasure Trips
As documented in Methodology, commuting accounts for only 29.9% of cycling trips (NTS) and 29.5% of cycling time (ALS), whereas leisure represents 39.7% of trips and 70.5% of minutes. Following Nellthorp et al. (2026) (§1.4.1, Table 2), appraisal must separate Exercise & Pleasure (marginal \(VTT = 0\), full Journey Ambience & health benefits, lower car-diversion MECs) from Other Non-Work Utility (shopping, education, station access). We propose a two-tier extension:

Tier 1 (Screening): Apply calibrated purpose multipliers (1.5× local leisure + 0.5× other utility on King's Sutton–Banbury adds +13.5 leisure and +4.5 other-utility trips/day to 8.97 commute trips).
Tier 2 (Full corridor): Run a spatial gravity model linking LSOAs, rail stations, and OSM campsites to greenway attractors with longer leisure decay (\(L \approx 6\text{–}9\text{ km}\)) calibrated to rural trail counters.



4.3 Behavioural Ramp-Up Convolved with AMAT Health Lags
Over ATE’s 40-year appraisal period (3.5% transport / 1.5% health discounting; Nellthorp et al. (2026) §2.3; HM Treasury (2026)), AMAT applies 100% demand in Year 1 plus a 5-year linear physiological health lag. Because real-world route uptake builds over 3–8 years (Goodman et al. 2014), we convolve a Bass diffusion S-curve (Bass 1969) with AMAT’s 5-year health lag (equations in Appendix §4).








Figure 3: 40-year trajectory (2030–2069) on King’s Sutton–Banbury (Corridor Central): (A) annual commute trips under instant jump vs 3-, 5-, and 8-yr Bass ramp-up; (B) effective health-benefit share after convolving behavioural adoption with AMAT’s 5-yr health lag.

Because 86% of core commute PVB sits in Health and Journey Ambience, all outputs will enforce Nellthorp et al. (2026) (Table 13) double-counting rules via the 4-table hand-off schema in Appendix §5:






ImportantDouble-Counting Compliance Summary (Nellthorp et al. 2026, Table 13)




User benefits vs health (Recs 1–2): Retain \(\theta \approx 0\) so Journey Ambience and AMAT/TATE3030 health benefits remain additive.
Rule of a Half (§2.4): Apply RoH only to \(\Delta CS\) / Journey Ambience — never halve physical-activity health benefits or MECs.
User benefits vs safety (Recs 3–6): Journey Ambience (16.28 p/min) embeds users’ perceived safety WTP; add only external casualty outcomes and mode-shift safety MECs.
Place quality (Recs 7–10): Value origin/destination place quality only for dwell/movements strictly outside modelled trips.
Exercise & Pleasure VTT (§1.4.1): Set marginal \(VTT = 0\) for Exercise & Pleasure trips while retaining Journey Ambience and health benefits.

title: RailActive Data Dictionary & Dataset Register
text:
This document defines the machine-readable data dictionary and datasets register for the RailActive project and application.
The register standardizes data structures, variable names, units, and licensing across active datasets (North-South Corridor, custom GPX re-alignments, OS OpenRoads, DfT STATS19 road safety, OpenStreetMap active travel infrastructure, and the National Cycle Network), while tracking dependencies for forthcoming datasets (trip attractors, LCWIPs, OSMRN/PSGA, and OS NGD pavements).
Underlying schemas are version-controlled and available for download:

data/datasets_overview.csv: High-level dataset catalog and status
data/data_dictionary.csv: Full variable schema and technical definitions
data/data_dictionary.json: Web-ready JSON format consumed by the frontend

title: Appraisal & Spatial Modeling Methodology
text:
The RailActive appraisal framework integrates spatial network analysis with empirical demand modeling and the UK Department for Transport’s (DfT) Active Mode Appraisal Toolkit (AMAT), aligned with Active Travel England’s Active Mode Benefits: Theoretical Framework (Nellthorp et al. 2026). For the first-principles uptake specification and Oxfordshire–Uxbridge case study, see the Uptake Modelling Decision Brief.
The workflow comprises three interlinked analytical stages:

Spatial Network Categorisation: Ingestion and classification of civil engineering haul roads, access tracks, and intersecting rights of way.
Empirical Demand Segmentation: Calibrating baseline active travel uptake across utility (commuting, education, shopping) and leisure purposes using the National Travel Survey (NTS) and Active Lives Survey (ALS).
Multi-Modal Economic Appraisal: Quantifying 15 appraisal components across health, economy, environment, and capital costs following official TAG guidance.

title: Appraisal & Spatial Modeling Methodology
text:
2 Travel Demand & Trip Purpose Modeling
Traditional transport appraisal tools frequently focus solely on the commute-to-work (e.g. Census Journey to Work matrices or the Propensity to Cycle Tool). For a national or regional spine route like the HS2 corridor, this introduces a severe undercounting risk.

2.1 Empirical Insights from National Datasets
Analysis of recent microdata from the UK Data Service reveals the true distribution of active travel in England:

National Travel Survey (NTS, 2022–2024):

Leisure Cycling (39.7%): The single largest purpose for cycling, outstripping commuting (29.9%).
Leisure Walking (57.9%): Walking for leisure or exercise (“just walk”) accounts for 42.5% of walking trips, whereas commuting walking represents only 6.7%.
Trip Distance & Duration: Leisure cycle trips average 4.20 miles (6.76 km) and 29.9 minutes, compared to 3.43 miles (5.52 km) and 22.9 minutes for commuting. Leisure cyclists spend 31% more time per journey exercising.

Sport England Active Lives Survey (ALS, Year 9, 2023–2024):

Participation: 31.9% of adults cycle for leisure and sport annually, compared to 11.3% for travel.
Activity Volume: Leisure accounts for 70.5% of total cycling minutes and 61.5% of total walking minutes across the population.

title: Appraisal & Spatial Modeling Methodology
text:
3 Economic Benefits Appraisal (DfT AMAT)
Economic benefits are evaluated using a concise, verified base-R implementation of AMAT (railactive/amat).

3.1 Appraisal Components

Premature Death Reduction (Health):

Uses the WHO Health Economic Assessment Tool (HEAT) dose-response curve adapted for TAG:

\[\text{RR} = \max\left(0.55, \exp\left(\frac{\ln(0.90)}{11.25} \times \text{MET-hours/week}\right)\right)\]

Attributable deaths avoided are calculated across 5 age bands for males and females and valued using discounted Years of Life Lost (YLL) at £92,240 per life-year.

Workplace Absenteeism:

Sickness absence reduction (0.25 days per user per year) applied to employed new users, valued at average regional daily labor output (£267.36/day).

Journey Ambience & Quality:

Valued using the Rule of a Half for existing users and new switchers:

\[\text{Benefit} = \left(\text{Trips}_{\text{existing}} + \frac{\text{Trips}_{\text{new}}}{2}\right) \times \Delta\text{Rate} \times \text{Time on Scheme} \times \text{VoT}_{\text{non-work}}\]

Upgrading from “No provision” to “Off-road segregated cycle track” yields an amenity improvement of 16.28 p/min.

Decongestion & Environmental Externalities:

Mode-shift from private cars and taxis reduces vehicle-kilometres:

\[\text{Vehicle-km Reduced} = \text{Trips}_{\text{new}} \times \text{Trip Length} \times \text{Days} \times \left(\frac{\text{Car Divert}}{\text{Car Occupancy}} + \frac{\text{Taxi Divert}}{\text{Taxi Occupancy}}\right)\]

Savings are calculated across 7 marginal external cost streams: highway congestion, infrastructure wear, collision risk, local air quality (\(PM_{2.5}\), \(NO_x\)), ambient noise, greenhouse gas emissions (\(CO_2e\)), and indirect taxation losses.

title: RailActive Project Documentation
text:
RailActive investigates the potential to repurpose High Speed Two (HS2) construction assets—including haul roads, access tracks, and maintenance strips—into a high-quality, segregated, multi-user active travel spine.
The corridor stretches from London Euston / Old Oak Common through the Colne Valley, Chilterns, and rural Midlands into Birmingham Curzon Street, with wider strategic feeder links extending toward the North West (805.6 km total network in v0.5.2).
Key project aims include:

Infrastructure Repurposing: Identifying where temporary construction access roads and haul tracks can be permanently retained for cycling, walking, and wheeling.
Severance Reduction: Overcoming historical and modern transport barriers (motorways, rail corridors, rivers) to reconnect fragmented rural communities.
Empirical Demand Modeling: Integrating commute, school, and leisure trip generators to estimate uptake.
Economic Benefits Appraisal: Applying the Department for Transport’s (DfT) Active Mode Appraisal Toolkit (AMAT) and ATE’s Active Mode Benefits: Theoretical Framework (Nellthorp et al. 2026) to quantify decongestion, health mortality, workplace absenteeism, and journey ambience benefits.

title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Technical Appendix
text: This technical appendix accompanies the Oxfordshire–Uxbridge Decision Brief. It documents the audit of existing railactive prototype scripts, the full PCT logistic and temporal ramp-up equations, supplementary corridor diagnostics, and the standardised 4-table hand-off schema for economic appraisal.

title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Technical Appendix
section: 1 Audit of Existing RailActive Prototype Work
text:
1 Audit of Existing RailActive Prototype Work
Before specifying the appraisal-ready pipeline, we audited analytical outputs across railactive/pipeline, railactive/hs2cycle, and railactive/amat:

Harmonised corridor alignment (north_south_corridor_v2.json, v0.5.2): 805.6 km preferred North–South Greenway spine (385.7 km core HS2 alignment plus Avenue Verte and Stoke–Birkenhead branches) with a 3-tier status taxonomy (preferred, alternative, superseded) and civil-asset classes (Repurposed HS2 TCR, HS2 delivered greenway, Dual Use MATs).
Multi-purpose network assignment (pipeline Phases 1–4): Splicing the preferred greenway into a 1.72M-link corridor network in Rust/CSIS netassign (with DEM gradients capped at \(\pm 2\%\) on engineered alignments) and validating against 7,219 cycling and 1,439 walking counters lifted baseline cycling fit from \(R^2_{\log 10} = 0.352\) (commute-only) to \(0.676\) (56.2% within \(2\times\)), and walking fit from \(-0.177\) to \(0.488\). Phase 2 separated route diversion (+3,175 bike pkm/day) from induced/shifted commute demand (+4,953 bike pkm/day); Phase 4 lifted spine cycling from 86.7 to 132.3 riders/day (+52.6%).
Verified AMAT engine (railactive/amat): Pure base-R DfT AMAT implementation (May 2026 TAG / 2023 prices) matching the official Clifton Road worked example to £0.00 across every stream (BCR = 2.840169).

Five structural prototype gaps must be resolved before full-corridor business-case modelling (Table 1):




Table 1: Methodological audit of existing railactive prototype uptake scripts and required upgrades.












#
Current Prototype Implementation
Economic / Appraisal Risk
Required Upgrade




1
Ad-hoc commute uplift (Phase 2): heuristic proximity multipliers (+35% cyclists; up to 7.5% car shift)
Violates joint modelling-valuation alignment: demand does not respond to the same GC attributes valued in appraisal.
Anchor uptake in a transparent GC / logistic propensity specification with corridor-exposure attenuation (omega_ij).


2
Unseparated leisure uplift (Phase 4): hardcoded trail (5.0x vs 2.5x) and campsite weights without separating diversion vs generation
Risks over-crediting leisure generation and mixes Exercise & Pleasure (VTT = 0) with Other Non-Work Utility.
Segment outputs into TAG’s four active-mode trip purposes and separate route reassignment from net generation.


3
Static steady-state flows: single daily flow; AMAT applies 100% demand in Year 1 plus 5-yr physiological health lag
Overstates PVB by 10-25% if real-world uptake builds over 3-8 years.
Convolve an explicit Bass behavioural adoption S-curve with AMAT’s 5-year physiological health lag over 40 years.


4
Census 2021 lockdown distortion: Phase 2 used March 2021 OD matrices (~31% WFH)
Distorts inter-town commuting patterns along rural corridors.
Benchmark against 2011 Census OD (pre-COVID, PCT-compatible), then apply a post-COVID hybrid-working scalar.


5
Unbridged demand-to-AMAT schema: link flows omit OD trip lengths, prop_on_scheme, diversion shares, and e-bike splits
Economists cannot populate AMAT or TATE3030 without ad-hoc post-processing.
Export a formal 4-table hand-off schema with built-in double-counting checks.

title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Technical Appendix
text:
2 PCT Logistic Propensity Specification
Under Random Utility Maximisation (RUM), commute cycling share \(p_{ij}\) on \((i, j)\) follows a logistic function of utility difference \(\Delta V_{ij} = -\lambda\,(GC^{\text{cycle}}_{ij} - GC^{\text{alt}}_{ij})\):
\[
\text{logit}\bigl(p_{ij}\bigr) = \ln\!\left(\frac{p_{ij}}{1 - p_{ij}}\right) = \alpha(q_{ij}) + f(d_{ij},\, g_{ij})
\tag{1}\]
In the UK Propensity to Cycle Tool (Lovelace et al. 2017), calibrated on 2011 Census OD flows across England and Wales, the baseline distance–hilliness decay function for fastest-route distance \(d_{ij}\) (km) and average gradient \(g_{ij}\) (%) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{logit}\bigl(p^{\text{base}}_{ij}\bigr) &= -3.818 - 0.652\,d_{ij} + 2.084\sqrt{d_{ij}} + 0.00878\,d_{ij}^2 \\
&\quad - 0.256\,g_{ij} + 0.0199\,d_{ij}g_{ij} - 0.123\sqrt{d_{ij}}\,g_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
Area-wide transformation to Go Dutch shifts the infrastructure-quality intercept (\(\Delta \alpha_{\text{Dutch}} = +2.552\), with slope term \(-0.079\,d_{ij}\)), while E-bikes additionally attenuates distance and gradient exertion penalties \(e(t)\) (Nellthorp et al. 2026, sec. 4.2.3).

title: Active Travel Uptake Modelling: Technical Appendix
text:
4 Temporal Adoption & Health-Lag Equations
Cumulative behavioural adoption \(r(t) \in [0, 1]\) at \(t\) years post-opening follows a Bass diffusion S-curve (Bass 1969) with innovation parameter \(p\) and imitation parameter \(q\):
\[
r(t) = \frac{1 - e^{-(p + q)t}}{1 + \frac{q}{p}\,e^{-(p + q)t}}
\tag{3}\]
In appraisal year \(y \ge oy\) (mid-year \(t_y = y - oy + 0.5\)), daily trips equal:
\[
\Delta T_y = \Delta T^{*} \cdot r(t_y) \cdot (1 + g_{\text{bg}})^{\min(y - oy,\, 20)}
\tag{4}\]
where \(\Delta T^{*}\) is steady-state uptake and \(g_{\text{bg}} = 0.0075\) is AMAT’s annual background growth rate. Convolving annual conversion cohorts \(\Delta r_j = r(t_j) - r(t_{j-1})\) with AMAT’s 5-year linear physiological mortality lag gives the effective health-benefit share \(H^{\text{eff}}_k\) in operational year \(k\):
\[
H^{\text{eff}}_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \Delta r_j \cdot \min\!\bigl(1,\; 0.2\,(k - j + 1)\bigr)
\tag{5}\]
Sensitivity profiles evaluated in the main brief use \((p=0.22, q=0.70)\) for Fast (3-yr), \((p=0.10, q=0.55)\) for Central (5-yr), and \((p=0.05, q=0.35)\) for Slow (8-yr) maturity.
